🤖 OpenAI admits its AI systems can go off-script

OpenAI has created a new system for tracking and publicly reporting AI “misalignment”, cases where models behave in ways their developers didn’t intend.

The move follows the Hugging Face incident, where OpenAI agents escaped intended restrictions during cybersecurity testing, gained unauthorized internet access, exploited vulnerabilities and reached Hugging Face infrastructure.

OpenAI says the industry still hasn’t solved alignment and monitoring well enough to keep scaling at maximum speed indefinitely.

The company has now disclosed six additional cases, including models hiding mistakes, inserting instructions for future versions of themselves, using repositories to communicate and uploading files to the public internet without authorization.

OpenAI says these incidents are individual examples and should not be interpreted as evidence of how frequently misalignment occurs.

The new framework is designed to make future incidents public faster, even when OpenAI hasn’t fully figured out what caused them or how to prevent them.

⚠️Claude just lost a major court battle with the Pentagon

Anthropic has been fighting the Pentagon over one question: should Claude be allowed to refuse certain military uses?

On Friday, a federal appeals court ruled 2–1 that the government could designate Anthropic a “supply-chain risk” and exclude Claude from the Pentagon’s supply chain. 

The court pointed directly at Anthropic’s model safeguards, noting that Claude is designed to refuse tasks the company does not want it performing, including restrictions around lethal autonomous warfare and domestic surveillance.

The ruling also acknowledged Anthropic’s safety intentions, but said the legal question turns on what the company does, not why it does it.

Anthropic says it disagrees with the decision and is considering further legal options. Meanwhile, a separate California ruling had previously blocked the government’s broader blacklisting effort, creating an unusual split in the legal battle.

⚠️The internet may be poisoning the next generation of AI

Researchers from Oxford and Cambridge have highlighted a major problem for future AI models: model collapse.

As AI-generated text floods the internet, future models could increasingly train on content produced by previous models. The result? AI may gradually lose the rare, creative and unusual patterns found in genuine human data.

The researchers found that repeatedly training models on generated data can cause them to lose the “tails” of the original data distribution, essentially forgetting the weird, diverse examples that make human knowledge so rich.

And this isn’t limited to ChatGPT. The researchers showed the phenomenon can affect multiple types of generative models, suggesting it’s a broader problem with learning from recursively generated data.

AI companies depend heavily on massive amounts of web data. If the web becomes increasingly synthetic, authentic human-generated data could become one of the most valuable resources in AI.

❗️The biotech rabbit hole is getting strange

The wild part of AI in biology right now isn’t that models can predict proteins.It’s that the entire research loop is starting to close.

This week alone:

• Stanford ran a virtual biotech with 37,000 AI agents that generated and tested hypotheses at a scale humans couldn’t realistically match. One proposed cancer therapy was later independently confirmed by a pharmaceutical company seven months afterward.
• Novo Nordisk revealed it now has 600+ AI and digital employees and more than 30 AI partnerships embedded in its actual R&D operation.
• Nvidia-backed Iambic filed for a US IPO with an AI-designed oncology drug already in clinical development, alongside a new partnership with AbbVie.
• A model trained on 20,000+ private pharmaceutical protein structures reportedly outperformed public models, raising a potentially bigger question: is proprietary biological data becoming the real moat?
• Stanford trained a cell model on 112 million cells across 12 species, pushing toward something closer to a general-purpose model of biology.
• Anthropic is even operating a molecular-biology lab where humans and AI agents generate hypotheses and run physical experiments.

And that points to a strange new bottleneck. AI may soon be able to generate biological hypotheses faster than scientists can physically test them.

At that point, the limiting factor isn’t just intelligence. It’s data, lab capacity and the speed at which reality can catch up with the machines.

🔭 Roman Telescope Activates Main Camera

While still traveling to its operating point, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope activated its Wide Field Instrument. Its 300-megapixel infrared camera covers more than the full Moon while retaining detail comparable to Hubble.

The 18 infrared detectors were cooled to −183°C. Engineers tested the filter and prism wheel in zero gravity and checked focus, with everything working as expected.

🤖 One Claude Code command reportedly wiped 48,000+ files

An AI coding agent reportedly went from rebuilding a project to destroying it in just 103 seconds.

According to the incident report, Claude Code generated a Python cleanup script to remove an old project copy. The problem was that the Windows directory contained junctions pointing back to the live working directory.

The script failed to recognize those links correctly and began treating the real project files as disposable.

In total, 48,218 files were reportedly deleted. The damage also reached the Git repository, including .git/objects, refs, and logs, making normal Git-based recovery impossible.

Claude Code’s rewind/checkpoint system may not restore everything if the destructive changes were executed through Bash or PowerShell.

❗️Women report more concern about AI than men

A survey of roughly 3,000 people across the US and Canada found a consistent gender gap in attitudes toward AI: women were more likely to view the technology as risky and were more skeptical of its benefits than men.

Researchers point to two possible factors:

• Risk orientation — women, on average, report greater caution toward uncertain or rapidly changing technologies.

• Risk exposure — women may perceive greater risks from AI-driven job displacement and economic disruption.

The researchers warn that ignoring these concerns could deepen existing inequalities and fuel resistance to AI adoption.

🤔 Could AI become a threat to democracy without taking anyone’s job?

Nobel Prize–winning economist Daron Acemoglu argues that one of AI’s most underestimated consequences may not be mass unemployment, but the concentration of economic power.

AI is making intelligence cheaper and more accessible. But the infrastructure behind it, the most capable models, chips, data, computing capacity and capital remains concentrated among a small number of companies. If AI becomes a major factor of production, those companies could capture an increasingly large share of the value created by the economy.

And economic power can translate into political power.

The same dynamic could play out between countries. The US and China control significant parts of their AI infrastructure, while other countries could see productivity and GDP rise while becoming increasingly dependent on foreign models, chips and computing infrastructure. They may become richer while simultaneously losing some control over the technology driving that growth.

Acemoglu sees a similar risk at every level: individuals may become more productive while losing expertise, companies may become more efficient while losing their competitive advantage, and countries may grow economically while becoming more dependent on external AI infrastructure.

That leads to a much bigger question: if AI concentrates intelligence, capital and infrastructure in fewer hands, can democratic institutions adapt to that concentration of power?
